About this work

De Laudibus Sanctissimae Matris Annae — "In Praise of the Most Holy Mother Anne" — is Trithemius's treatise honouring St Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary. He wrote it at Sponheim with a dedicatory letter to Rumold Laupach dated 1 July 1494; it circulated with commendatory poems on the Holy Kindred, the extended family of Christ that the late-medular devotion to Anne had made its centre. It is a characteristic piece of his early Marian-hagiographic output.

This is the Leipzig edition, ca. 1497 (BSB scan) — a reprint of the 1494 Mainz first edition. It is one of six witnesses of De Laudibus Sanctissimae Matris Annae in this corpus (prdl-24364, prdl-24366, prdl-24367, prdl-70283, prdl-70284). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No published English translation is known;

    In Praise of the Most Holy Mother Anne

    A very useful treatise on the praises of the most holy mother Anne, by Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of the divine Father Benedict.

    The Most Elegant Book of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, on the Praises of the Most Holy Mother Anne.

    The opening of the book treats of the praises of Saint Anne in general. Chapter 1.

    The author’s invocation of divine help, to God and the saints. Chapter 2.

    An exhortation to all the faithful that they should honor Saint Anne. Chapter 3.

    Against those who assail the memory of Saint Anne. Chapter 4.

    Why God chose Saint Anne from eternity to be a parent. Chapter 5.

    How holy and pleasing to God her life always was. Chapter 6.

    Why Anne conceived her daughter without sin. Chapter 7.

    How mother Anne offered her daughter to God. Chapter 8.

    Why the holy mother Anne is held in great honor with God. Chapter 9.

    Why she has power to come to the aid of our miseries. Chapter 10.

    Why she must be held by us in the greatest reverence. Chapter 13.

    Letter of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, concerning the book on the praises of the most holy Anne.

    To the venerable and most religious father, Lord Rumold Laupach, prior of the Frankfurt convent of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, Johannes of Trittenheim, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin in Sponheim, of the Order of the divine Father Benedict: greeting and charity.

    Desiring, excellent father, to satisfy our own wish and your requests, we have written, with sincere devotion, a book on the praises of the most holy mother Anne, which we dedicate to your name, since you seemed to us worthy before others, as being a very great worshipper and most devoted lover of the same venerable Anne. From the history, however, which is sufficiently widespread, we have taken nothing, or little, because it seemed to us less approved, and in very many places apocryphal. Yet we did not wish to refute it, lest we give simple people occasion for murmuring if, as they themselves think, we were to attack with new presumption what has been approved by antiquity. Therefore we left the history untouched, and those things that had been known by most evident faith, truth, and reason, by the gift of God, we have brought together for the honor of the holy mother Anne. We have also excluded the miracles of Saint Anne from this volume, lest we make our treatise suspect to learned men, who do not readily give credence to these things. Therefore, if it should happen that you hesitate about anything, write back: you will find us ready, who will demonstrate to you and to all men the reason for each of the things we have written. After the end of this work we have added certain poems on the praises of the saint, which were sent to us at Basel by learned men on the other side. From Sponheim, on the Kalends of July, in the year [unclear].

    Here begins the treatise of Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, on the praises of the venerable and most blessed Anne, mother of the Mother of God.

    Necessity compels me, and devotion of mind presses me, to write, according to the powers of my talent, the praises of the most blessed Anne, mother of the Mother of God, for the edification of the faithful, and to proclaim in truthful narration with how great compassion she has been accustomed to aid the wretched. But when I consider the poverty of my talent, unclean as I am I fear to speak of the most holy one. For with how great praise is she worthy, who bore the Mother of God? What discourse will unfold it? Therefore I wish to fashion something in honor of so great a mother, and I am afraid, because whatever I shall say is less than her praises; whatever I shall write is far beneath the majesty of the matter. Indeed, when I recall to memory her benefits toward the wretched, I cannot be silent from her praises, even if I wish to be. Hence her very great compassion has brought forth my vow, stirred devotion, and requires the offering of honor. A devout also, lest I say importunate, request of friends impelled me no less to dare it; from their faith and prayer our weakness has received confidence. Therefore, although I know myself to be a sinner, although I am not sufficient worthily to praise the most holy parent of the Queen of Heaven, nevertheless I ought by no means to withdraw from the proposed praise, lest I seem to have incurred the vice of ingratitude.

    I shall attempt, according to my devotion, what I can, for no one is required by God to do what he cannot; no one before the eternal Judge is judged empty of good will. Therefore I, a man, shall praise the goddess; a servant, the lady; a sinner, the most holy one. For he did not restrain sinners from the praise of God who said in the Psalm: Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. Indeed, when he urges the nations to praise the Lord, what else does he do but call sinners? For they were far from justice, because they worshiped not God but idols. Therefore no one is permitted to be silent from the praises of God, since even idolatrous nations are called to repentance. Let all, therefore, who receive his mercy praise the Lord; let all who live in the flesh praise him, because he himself is the one who created all, he himself who gave life. Let the righteous and the sinner praise together: the former because he has been preserved by the Lord’s mercy, lest he fall; the latter because even after [unclear], lest he perish eternally, he has been raised up.

    And if praise is not beautiful in the mouth of sinners, nevertheless a guilty conscience excuses no one from the praises of God, since by his mercy all are reserved for repentance. Let the righteous man bear praise, the sinner confession. Let the former praise because, with grace preserving him, he stood bravely; let the latter confess that, with mercy following after, he rose again. Praise the Lord, my soul; I shall praise my God in my life; I shall sing psalms to the Lord as long as I shall be. I shall open my mouth to confess to the Lord; likewise I shall prepare my mind and my pen:

    With what devotion I can, I shall sing the praises of the most blessed mother Anne. For if we are commanded to praise God generally in his saints, we are without doubt urged to honor his parents more especially. For he who commanded us to honor our parents by no means excludes his own according to the flesh. Therefore, dearest brothers, it is holy to offer the diligent praises of devotion to those from whose blood we believe the Son of God took flesh. Among them the most blessed Mother of God rightly holds the first place; so great are the merits of her holiness that she has been exalted in heaven above the choirs of angels. After her, the most holy Anne, her mother, of whom we have undertaken to speak, just as she is nearest in the flesh to the Son of God, so by the merits of her virtues she is believed to be acceptable before the other saints. Nor may it be permitted us to doubt her holiness, since we believe that she bore the Mother of God without the stain of original guilt. For she could not have been the mother of so great a virgin unless she was holy, through whose virginal birth we received the remedies of eternal salvation. Anne is the holy root; Mary the Virgin, the most holy tree; the fruit is the Son of God, the medicine of souls. A good tree, a holy tree, a tree most fruitful without human cultivation, which took its beginning from a holy root and its growth from the richness of the heavenly rain. Never does a good root produce a bad tree; never does a good tree bear bad fruits. A good tree cannot stand without a root, nor bear good fruit unless it is good. As a tree is known from its fruit, so what sort the mother is is declared in the daughter. In the most holy Mother of God we understand what we ought to think about the holiness of her mother. A birth free from the guilt of original stain did not befit any mother except a holy one; to conceive and bear the Mother of God was fitting for none except one most pleasing to God and, above all then living in Israel, devout. For that she loved God above all things is shown by the first instruction of her daughter. As a little child, she is read to have been entrusted to the Lord; she is recorded to have served God in the temple; conceived without any guilt, she is believed always to have lived holy in the world. What more do you require? Is such an excellent life of the daughter from infancy not sufficient to declare the merits of the mother? If Anne had not been most holy, she would never have instructed her daughter so carefully and devoutly for the honor of God. We know that such as mothers are, such also are their daughters as instructed by them. But the most blessed mother Anne, just as in merit and holiness she surpasses all women, so she took care to instruct her daughter from youth, more diligently than all the saints, in the love of God. If, therefore, we love the Son of God, if we honor his most pure Mother, why do we grow lukewarm and keep silence from the praise of his most holy grandmother and mother Anne? If we seek the honor of the highest king, why do we not love his parents? He who despises the lineage of the emperor does injury to the king. If we love Jesus Christ, the emperor of all, if we fear his divine majesty, it is fitting that we honor his venerable grandmother, from whose

    from [unclear] womb, without the seed of a man, we believe without doubt that he came forth. Whatever praise we bestow upon her veneration, let us firmly believe pertains to the honor of the highest King. For the honor of the most holy mother Anne, let all the faithful come together. Render praises to the most high Lord in memory of her; for reverence of her, rejoice with religious devotion. I, who have experienced many of her benefits, [say that] you will have her as a ready advocate in every tribulation, if you celebrate her memory with faithful devotion. Therefore she is to be honored by all, by whose merits the Son of God grants all things at her nod; whose honorable name the court of the heavenly citizens honors with the greatest reverence; whom the queen of heaven, the mother of God, observes as her sweetest parent. Whoever has chosen her as patroness, whoever has persevered devoutly in her service, he shall be saved both now and forever. For all the benefits that the Son of God is accustomed to grant to mortals through his beloved mother, he cannot deny to the merits of his grandmother; indeed, at times he bestows greater things through her, so that he may draw us, as if by gifts, to the memory of her, long neglected. Nor can the Son of God ever despise his own parents, who commanded us so earnestly to honor the parents of others.

    The author’s invocation to God and Saint Anne and all the heavenly ones, that they may bring the grace of writing. Chapter 2.

    God, true light, who illuminates every man coming into this world; God, who justifies the impious and calls sinners to repentance; God, who gives wisdom to little ones and makes eloquent the tongues of those who stammer: grant me, I beseech you, forgiveness for my sins; grant me wisdom for your praise; grant me light by which I may understand, know, and love you, and be so conquered by love for most blessed Anne that I may worthily embrace her praises in this work. God, who for the thirsty people in the desert brought forth water from the hardest rock, soften the hardness of my heart, so that I may be able to praise you in your saints, in the grandmother of your Son, in the parents of your only-begotten, with such devotion of mind that, through your mercy and her intercession, it may profit unto devotion not only for me but also for all who read this little night-work of ours. God, who opened the mouth of a beast so that it uttered human words against an unwise man, graciously water the dryness of my tongue by the infusion of your grace; strengthen my trembling hand with the Holy Spirit, so that concerning most holy Anne I may write nothing except what is right, persuade nothing except what is holy, and utter nothing except what is worthy. Grant me, I ask, almighty and eternal God, the aid of heavenly grace in this work, you who gave me the resolve to will it. For I am a worm and not a man, wretched and unhappy, sold under sin.

    I, who am not worthy to lift up my face to the heavens because of the multitude of my iniquity, how much less should I dare to touch the praises of most blessed Anne with impure lips. Yet by your grace I am what I am, and all the good that I will and am able to do. For you, Lord, enlighten the will by your grace, that it may will good things and be made good. You also are he who grants us to work for a good will. In all things we acknowledge your grace going before our will, and in the good things that we will and do we proclaim your gifts, without any merits of ours. Nothing comes from us except evil; nothing proceeds from you except good.

    Since, therefore, I can do nothing good of myself without your grace, I devoutly flee to you; I appeal to you in humble subjection, that what my merits impede, you may mercifully bestow by the gift of your grace. Give me, Lord, wisdom, the attendant of your seats, that she may be with me and labor with me at all times, and especially in this work in which, with slender powers, I have resolved to praise your name in holy mother Anne.

    You also, Anne, most holy mother, whose memory is being treated, deign in your wonted kindness to be present with me, that I may be made fit to set forth your praises, and may be found a faithful herald of your merits. My lady, my hope, my advocate in every tribulation, now mercifully be present to one who desires to praise you; and since by manifold kindness you have stirred up the will to write, obtain by your merits ability for my poor talent, that it may be sufficient to praise you worthily. I seek nothing except your honor. I desire nothing except to please you. I intend to write nothing about your praises except what is right and true. Therefore, I pray, bring help; give the hand of assistance; obtain grace.

    You also, immaculate Mother of God, who taught your servants to honor Anne, your venerable mother, be present to me, who desire to set forth her praises, by your merits, so that the devotion of your servant may obtain in the work the due effect which the grace of God conceived in the mind. You also, blessed spirits of the heavenly fatherland, who exult in the most sacred fruit of mother and daughter, the virgin, our Lord Jesus Christ, make me by your prayers a worthy praiser of Anne, and obtain for me the grace of the Holy Spirit. If you honor mother and daughter in heavenly joy, it is fitting that you assist their praisers in this pilgrimage.

    You also, most blessed Anne’s devoted worshippers, do not detract from our pious studies, but if in anything we have failed through weakness, excuse it through charity. Nothing is written by me through contention or vain glory. Nothing of apocryphal doubtful character is alleged; nothing is assumed except what has been approved. I receive nothing that opposes the divine ordinances. I write nothing that stains the Christian faith. I introduce nothing that does not accord with holy morals.

    Let no one, therefore, more learned detract from me as I praise you, Anne; let no equal disparage me; let no inferior mock me. What is true prevails, and what proceeds from the true does not fail. Let no one think me contemptible on my own account as I write about this most holy woman. Let no one [unclear] my devotion. Let no one murmur against the praises of the holy mother Anne. I do not fear the barking of dogs; I do not fear the censures of the ignorant; I do not dread the torches of envy. For I write for the devout, not for the wicked; for the studious, not for the ignorant; for the humble, not for the proud. May the present work please those for whom it is written; may it profit those to whom it is offered; may it be of use to those to whom it is presented. What have I to do with those who are outside? What is it to me if they do not think rightly? What is it to me if they gnaw at holy things contrary to reason? I do not fear displeasing those whose censures and rash judgments I know.

    General exhortation to all the faithful.

    Hear me, you who love what is good and seek the Lord. I perform an embassy; I am led by devotion; I am driven by charity. The mother of the Mother of God has sent me, that I may proclaim her most holy merits. And now I come to you not with lofty speech, but as a simple man to the simple, as a devout man to the devout. If you are Christians, if you are good, if you love the grace of the Lord’s incarnation, why do you not love his ministers, that is, his parents? For they are those from whom the Son of God was born according to the flesh; if their way of life had not been most holy, it would by no means have been so acceptable to God. But when he willed his only-begotten Son to be born from them, he showed openly how holy and pleasing to himself they were. From these, one woman, most pleasing to God above all, chosen as the mother of the unique father, ever-virgin Mary, shone forth; she was borne without stain by the most blessed Anne, wife of Joachim, and was brought up by her most chastely in the fear of the Lord. The son of this most sacred Virgin is God, who redeemed us by his most holy passion. If you love the daughter, why do you not honor her mother? If there had been no mother, you would not have the daughter. To you, therefore, my discourse is now directed, you who dwell in the valley of tears. I address you, O sons of Adam, who are exiles from your homeland. I write to you who have been redeemed by the precious blood of the Son of God. I address you; I warn and exhort you that, if you love the Son of God, you should devoutly honor his kinsfolk according to the flesh. Among them, after his most holy mother, holy Anne is set before you as first of all to be honored; her holy merits are shown daily to the human race through many miracles. Take her as your patron; celebrate her memory more devoutly.

    if you wish to please God, the supreme ruler. Believe me, brothers, for I am about to speak the truth. If you love and honor the venerable mother with all your heart, you will know by experience how much the heavenly Emperor defers to her. She has such power with God that whatever she has asked of him, she is able to obtain without delay. Just as the King of heaven is believed to honor his own mother above all, so after her he venerates mother Anne before all the saints. And very often Anne obtains for her faithful ones what the daughter denies: not because she does not know how to grant what is asked, but so that, deferring to her mother, she may seem to call us to veneration of her. Thus also the supreme Emperor is moved to mercy by the prayers of the saints: not because he begins to will what before he did not will, but so that, deferring to his elect, he might instruct us in honoring them. For God is not moved in the human manner, nor is he ever stirred to anger from disturbance, but, always steadfast, wills what he wills; when he shows mercy at the prayers of the saints, he does not change his counsel, but mitigates the sentence. Therefore, to obtain God’s mercy, since our merits are not sufficient, the intercessions of the saints must be implored by us, so that what we cannot do by our own merits, [unclear] by theirs. Yet the citizens of the heavenly fatherland, even if they are unlike in the quality of their merits, nevertheless, in coming to the aid of our wretched condition, according to the variety of those who supplicate, if devotion demands it, are believed to be concordant in act and will; because, when the faith of the petitioner aids the advocate, it renders the merit for obtaining doubled. This, moreover, we attain not by conjecture but by experience. But when two blind men approach in supplication to some heavenly patron’s merit, one is given sight, the other is left in his blindness. No contempt of the saint is believed to be present, but the distrust of the suppliant is charged. Without faith devotion merits nothing. I have set these things forth with sure consideration, so that if anyone should not feel most blessed Anne to be present to him with as much readiness as we promise, he should not accuse us of falsehood, but recognize his own culpable distrust. For the greatest confidence before God and the saints is constant faith in their aid. Moreover, no Christian doubts that those who are more excellent in merits can do more before God. Therefore the most blessed mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, just as she surpasses all the saints in merits and holiness, so in power and majesty, as queen of heaven, she is rightly believed to excel them all. At her right hand, so to speak, we trust that her most blessed mother stands, whose life we know was most holy. There was not in Israel another holier than she, who in the conception of the mother of God constructed for the Holy Spirit a vessel without stain. Finally, if Elizabeth, the mother of the Lord’s forerunner, is believed to have been filled with the Holy Spirit and ineffable joy, how great an exultation, joy, and grace must have been fitting for the most holy mother of the parent of God, one is compelled [to say]. As much as a king differs from a soldier, so much, in its own way, [belongs] to Anne

    The merits are rightly preferred to the gifts of Elizabeth. Saint Elizabeth bore a soldier; Anna, the mother of God. There is no comparison where there is no likeness. If Elizabeth was full of grace because of John, much more do I believe that Anna obtained grace because of Mary. Anna was holy before she conceived the mother of God, yet in the conception she was more fully sanctified, since she deserved to become the tabernacle of her who, above all creatures, was full of grace. We call a casket or ark in which the pledges of the saints are kept sanctified and honorable; how much more ought we to venerate as venerable Anna, in whom the mother of God lay without stain, honored and sanctifying. Truly holy is she who bore that one without the fault of original stain, than whom [unclear] of the saints will be confessed, because no one was ever holier. Truly holy is she who was chosen to be the mother of the mother of God before she was born. O womb never to be named without honor, in which the ark of God deserved to be fashioned without stain. Blessed the belly that carried the lady of heaven; happy the breasts that deserved to nurse the mother of God. Run, peoples, from every side, and from the merits of so great a patroness receive blessing. For indeed, if the holy devotion of the faithful is directed toward her, we believe that almighty God bestows great gifts upon mortals, and not less than he has been accustomed to give through daughters. Therefore you, O faithful peoples, who believe the daughter of Saint Anna to be the mother of God, who rest beneath the shadow of the holiness of both, if you desire to advance in the love of God, if you wish to come to the heavenly fatherland, do not neglect the memory of the most holy mother. For after the queen herself she is the most powerful in the hall of the heavenly emperor, because from her blood the Son of God took flesh from the virgin. From whatever tribulation you cry to her, you will find help. She has power to grant you all things that you can ask in faith. She heals the sick, cleanses crimes, gladdens the hearts of the sorrowful with holy exultation, calms sad things, smooths rough things, drives away the phantasms of demons. As ice is dissolved by fire, so by the merit of the most holy mother Anna the ancient enemy, fleeing, is thrown into confusion. Anna, ark of piety, drives away disgrace, preserves fair fame, and marvelously removes base love from the minds of her faithful. Therefore honor Anna, you who lead the toilsome life of this world. Anna obtains pardon for sinners, roots out vices, plants virtues. Anna cures illnesses, heals wounds, exterminates pestilence. Therefore honor this mother, O children, who is powerful to bring you into the sight of God; whoever has her as advocate before God will fear no adversities of this world. Whoever, therefore, desires to lead a tranquil and holy life on earth, whoever earnestly asks pardon for his sins, should never depart from the service of this most holy mother. For she rewards her worshippers in many ways even in this life, and prepares eternal gifts for them if they persevere. I was younger than I am, and I have never seen a servant devoted to Saint Anna abandoned by God, nor his reputation stained by shameful reproach.

    Accordingly I urge you, O men distinguished by learning and knowledge of letters, not to despise the devotion of the simple, nor to criticize the cult of the most holy mother Anna as something new, but rather to imitate it as far as you can. For I was not persuaded in vain to say these things. For there are among you, if I may say so with the peace of good men, some who, swollen with the stamp of pride, despise all the devotional exercises of the simple, scorn the miracles and examples of the saints as ravings, and think that nothing holy should be admitted which they do not prove by the arguments of the philosophers. All revelations shown by God to devout people they regard as lies or women’s dreams; they call the legends of the saints fables; and while they rashly proclaim their own learning, they shamelessly attack the great works of God. They also reject the treatises of the holy fathers and of devout people, because they do not bear Ciceronian eloquence in their defense, as though they were lacking in learning, and they despise the words of heavenly instruction because of the instruction of the simple. O fools and subverters, why do you deceive yourselves? Why, though you are Christians, do you despise ecclesiastical simplicity? The grace of God is not known in eloquence, but is acquired in holy simplicity. At the final judgment of God, Quintilian eloquence will not be required of you, but Christian life. Ornate speech is not rewarded by God, but humble devotion. There sophistical arguments will cease, when the secrets of hearts will be manifest. Then the simple and devout will appear in glory, and the learned proud in punishment. Behold, the unlearned simple arise and receive the kingdom of God in their devout simplicity, and you with your doctrines descend in pride and arrogance to hell. You believe that the reputation of your learning is enough for you, by which, after the example of the ancients, [unclear] immortality among posterity

    may acquire [unclear]. But let it be so: let what you seek come to pass; let your name and fame be proclaimed with praise in the world for as long as it shall stand. What will it profit you? Truly a foolish consolation, if you are praised where you will never be, and are tormented where you will remain always, without end. Therefore I admonish and counsel you: put away haughtiness, drive out madness, cast aside fear, so that you may be able to escape the torments of hell. For God resists the proud; he regards not learning, but humble devotion; he rewards not words, but deeds; not knowledge, but life; not doctrine, but conscience. Rather, change your purpose, and do not despise the devotion of the simple, but imitate it. No one understands the house of God except him who receives it. What, then, you do not understand, with what rashness do you tear apart? The gift of God is not enclosed under the reasoning of philosophy. Devotion is rare among the learned, because, while they trust in the profundity of their acquired doctrine, they withdraw farther from simple devotion.

    For the grace of God is not well received when it is examined by human curiosity. While savor is sought in speech, inward sweetness is lost. The Holy Spirit despises a proud dwelling. Therefore shut your rash mouths, restrain your badly eloquent tongues, and do not speak falsehood against the Lord. Do not tear apart the devotion of the simple, lest it be counted against you as a grave scandal. Let no one think me, as I say these things, an enemy of the good arts; let no one believe me a slanderer of the learned, since I have always cultivated and loved letters, have always been accustomed to honor learned men, and have sometimes defended them even to the point of hatred and persecution by the unskilled. But let those who seem learned in their own eyes beware, lest, by despising the devotion of the simple, they think that they ought to be called back from reverence for Saint Anne. But if any such men are to exist, I would believe no learned man to be among their number, since true learning is accustomed to assist devotion, not to rebuke it. Many very learned men also, still living today, exercising their talents magnificently in verse and prose, have dedicated them to the merits of Saint Anne.

    Chapter Four.

    Against those who tear apart, deride, and attack the feast and memory of Saint Anne.

    Hear and understand, whoever you are, who disparage the festive memory of the most holy mother Anne, who attack her honor with impious talkativeness, who blaspheme her devotees with rash presumption. What displeases you in the most holy mother of the Mother of God? Do you prove her degenerate? She is holy; she is beloved by God. Foolish and unwise man, who blame as faults the good in the servants of God which you ought to imitate; who withhold the honor owed to the saints; who persecute the devotees of most blessed Anne without cause. For you reproach them and say: Why do you take up new feasts, you who do not celebrate the ancient ones? Listen, profane man. Does the feast of Saint Anne seem new to you, which is proved from the ancient monuments of the old to be most ancient? If it is new, how could the holy fathers have celebrated it in antiquity? It is not new, in whose honor Saint Augustine is said to have composed an elegant sermon a thousand years ago. That cannot be new about which very ancient songs exist. Or how will that be able to be new whose golden name is found inserted in the most ancient calendars? But to you it is both new and rare, you who have never celebrated her memory. Nor can the memory of the most blessed mother Anne be new, whose house, in which she had been accustomed to live in antiquity, is read to have been consecrated as a church under her name not long after the Passion of the Lord. Near Lyon there is a monastery of our order on the Île Barbe, where in a certain very ancient chapel the body of blessed

    [unclear] of the most holy mother Anne rests with great reverence from the people, which Saint Longinus, soldier of Christ, is said first to have founded, and, bringing with him from Jerusalem those most precious relics, to have placed them in the same place. Very ancient records of this matter are found in the said monastery. Do these things seem new to you? Cease, then, to disparage the feast of the most holy mother; cease to tear with impious tooth at her most worthy cult. Do not spread personal hatred against all; do not, because of displeasure with a few, be angry with everyone; do not carry an injury from a man up against the heavenly ones. Why, perhaps injured by a man, do you call the saints of God into blame? Cease, I beseech you, cease wishing to exact vengeance for one man or a few from the most holy mother Anne. I do not want you to revile her sanctity; I do not want you to deprive her of her honor; I do not want you to assail the devotion of her servants. If a man sins against a man, God will be able to appease him; but he who sins against the saints of God, against the parents and son of God, against the mother of the mother of God, who will pray for him? How can he hope to have him propitious, who has offended his saints, and indeed the most holy? For Saint Anne is worthy of every honor, she who deserved to bear the Mother of God without stain of guilt; whoever lessens her honor does injury to God. Therefore rather, if you are wise, if you understand, withdraw from this folly of yours, flee from this false madness, turn aside from this most wicked blasphemy, and undertake repentance for your former error, so that through tears of compunction you may wash away so unspeakable a fault. But if you do not do this, if you persevere in your obstinacy, you will not hinder the will of God, but you will have a share in the lot of the devil. God has resolved to honor Saint Anne in his Church; who will prevent him? Behold, kings and princes celebrate the memory of Saint Anne with religious devotion; behold, faithful peoples everywhere invoke her name, and you with the devil waste away, are confounded, and rave in your envy. Monks and religious of both sexes, the whole clergy of the churches of God, celebrate the feast and memory of the holy mother Anne with singular devotion; and you, envious dog, presume to bark against all. Why do you bark impiously? Why do you mutter wickedly? Be silent, go away, withdraw; not without grave chastisement will this impiety of yours be punished. For whoever disparages the honor and sanctity of the most blessed mother Anne, whoever blasphemes her worshippers, will not depart from this life without confusion. He will be confounded with evil confusion before God and men; reproaches and the worst ignominies will cover his head; he will be wretched and pitiable, and there will be no one to grieve over his calamity, all the days that he shall be upon the earth. That Almighty God [unclear] Saint [unclear]

    ... he chose Anna as the mother of his mother before the foundation of the world. Chapter 5.

    Just as almighty God, before the foundation of the world, appointed the time at which he would be born in the flesh, so too from eternity he preordained the parents from whom he would be born. For the Son of God did not find his parents, but sent them before: he who, without time, ordained them for time did not come upon them by chance accident, but by a wondrous dispensation chose them beforehand from eternity. Therefore most blessed Anna could confidently say that which is written of the eternal wisdom of God: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. From eternity I was ordained, and from ancient times.” Before the foundation of the world she existed in the divine mind, made not by nature but by grace pre-[unclear].

    Worthy to be [unclear] and honored is she whom the grace of God, by going before, appointed as [unclear] of the mother, and by always preserving made most holy [unclear]. Truly holy and most worthy of every honor is the parent who provided for us a rule of holier life and brought forth from her own breast the fountain of inexhaustible piety. She could not have been anything but most holy, who bore so precious a treasure in her womb. She was the most noble ark of the covenant, shining with the adornment of all virtues, in which was hidden that vessel which was the true manna, the virgin who was to give birth. With how great honor must Anna’s womb be judged worthy, which, made God’s treasury, carried a treasure of inestimable price.

    There must be no doubting, dearest brothers, but it must be believed with firm devotion, that blessed Anna was then filled with ineffable joy, when she bore in her most blessed womb for nine months the future mother of God, made worthy by the Holy Spirit from her conception and preserved clean from every stain. O who can narrate the joys of that most holy mother Anna, which she sensibly perceived in her breast from the presence of the Holy Spirit? What voice can express, what tongue relate, what mortal mind of a wayfarer comprehend, with how much gladness and exultation the inmost parts of most blessed Anna were filled, when she merited to feel the grace of the Holy Spirit in the heart of her daughter not yet born?

    If Elizabeth is said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit at the presence of the soldier, that this happened more abundantly in venerable Anna is proved by many arguments. For the former bore in her womb the herald of the highest king; the latter, the mother. The former had conceived the soldier; the latter, the queen. John, conceived in the womb, was sanctified; Mary also, in conception, was preserved. Finally, the Holy Spirit, choosing Mary from the hour of conception as his most pure bride and dwelling in her, never afterward abandoned her, not even for a moment; but, always guarding and directing her, he illuminated her with a special gift above all mortals. We believe that the most blessed mother of this virgin shared in this most sacred illumination, not only when she was bearing the virgin still enclosed in her womb, but also at all times afterward [unclear].

    in the days in which she lived in the world. For truly, her whom the Holy Spirit had made a worthy parent for God he possessed not without the very greatest gifts of his grace. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us choose as our advocate her whom we have known from eternity always to have pleased holy God, and, venerating her daily, let us honor her with fitting praises. Let married people honor her, because by her most holy childbirth she consecrated marriage to the Lord, for whom she bore a mother without stain. Let widows and the continent praise her, because she prefigured the rule of that continence. Let virgins love her, because she bore a virgin of such holiness that no one holier ever shone forth. Let the righteous honor her, because by her own most holy manner of life she showed them the rule of righteousness. Let sinners venerate her, because she bore the mother of him who makes the righteous from sinners. Let all venerate her with the greatest love, because she brought forth the mother of him who came as redeemer for all. Let no one grow sluggish in her praises; let no one fail in love for her; let no one become lukewarm in her worship. Let all love her as a common mother; let all honor her as a public advocate. By her gift all received the common Savior. For she will obtain for us pardon of sins, from whose blood the fountain of mercy flowed forth bodily. Rise up before her, brothers, because she does not abandon those who hope in her; she relieves the oppressed; she sustains those who have been relieved; she protects widows; she mercifully [defends?] orphans and wards; she [unclear] the weak; she raises and heals the feeble; she confirms those raised up in virtue. It is impossible that she, praying for her devotees, should not be heard, who built from her own breast so precious a bridal chamber for almighty God.

    How just, holy, and acceptable to God was the life and conduct of the most blessed mother Anne. Chapter VI.

    Whoever has read through the memorials of the holy fathers with diligent devotion can discover with how great holiness the life of the most blessed mother Anne shone. Concerning her, the holy prelate Epiphanius composed certain things; he records that her life shone with such righteousness, innocence, and purity that she had no equal in Israel. Honorius too, priest of Autun, a holy and learned man, published in the Speculum Ecclesiae certain things in a lucid discourse on the praises of the holy mother Anne, and showed in brief summary how holy she always lived. Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, once a cultivator of Mount Carmel and of the Carmelite order, when he wrote to Pope Celestine I concerning the birth of the blessed Mother of God, Mary ever virgin, inserted many proclamations of praise concerning the life and conduct of Saint Anne. But what need is there for me to cite many unknown doctors, when blessed Jerome the priest, named throughout the whole world, is said to have written certain praiseworthy things on this very matter, which are held by many?

    Therefore the most blessed Anne, so far as her generation according to the flesh was concerned, was sprung from the tribe of David, from Bethlehem, with Stolanus as her father and Emerentia as her mother, parents religious and devout according to the decrees of the law, who nourished her, together with her sister Esmeria, in the fear of the Lord from infancy. Moreover Esmeria, her sister, bore Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist. Joachim of Nazareth, of the tribe of Judah, took Anne as wife; she bore a daughter, Mary, afterwards Mother of God and ever virgin. O Joachim and Anne, parents worthy of eternal memory, who, serving the Lord God in simplicity, offered an inestimable treasure. Who could suffice to praise these parents worthily? For truly, unless their life had been most holy, they would never have brought forth offspring so pleasing to the Lord.

    They were of moderate but sufficient substance, obtaining what was necessary from the pasturing of sheep and from agriculture. From these things they are said to have made three equal portions: one they gave to the temple, another to the poor, and the third they kept for themselves for domestic uses. As for their character, they were most diligent in the observance of the law, approved in the fear of the Lord, perfect in love of God and neighbor. They adorned the marriage-bed with the fullest virtues, in which they advanced so far that they pleased God and men. In concord, innocence, and piety they were of one mind, and rich in every virtue. Both derived their origin from the house of David; both were perfect before the Lord; both awaited the redemption of Israel with longing. Both from their earliest age had been instructed in the fear of the Lord; both were dear to God; both were chosen to be the parents of the Mother of God. Anne, however, is believed to have been filled with greater grace, without disparagement to her husband, in whose venerable womb the most holy Mother of God was being formed without any stain. In her breast the love of God found for itself a gracious dwelling; from her blood the Holy Spirit built for the Son of God a most pure tabernacle. Worthy parent of the worthiest parent, who first of all [unclear] of our Savior's

    [unclear] the coming. To her, O brothers, direct the eyes of your mind; listen to the pattern of her life, and imprint your conduct with her footsteps. Do you wish to know what sort of woman she was? Turn over the writings of the aforesaid fathers. She was dignified in gait, calm with a countenance of shining grace, mature in counsel, composed in speech, most holy in worship and deed. On the law of the Lord she meditated day and night, firm in faith, strong in hope, filled with twofold charity. She had learned always to persist in prayers, and with the greatest longing she awaited the coming of the Lord. She was honorable in deed, sober in conduct, humble in mind. No one ever found her running about through streets and squares; no one heard her chattering uselessly in the houses of neighboring women; no one ever found that she had stood by at dances and spectacles. She learned from her youth to remain at home. She was accustomed to work at something with her hands. She did not seek to be seen outside by men. She strove to keep concord in good and peace with her neighbors. She did wrong to no one; by word or deed she disturbed no one. She was rarely seen in public. She did not sit in the squares with little women chattering, and she did not stand in the conversation of slanderers. For that most prudent woman knew that sin is not absent from much speaking; therefore with all watchfulness she guarded her heart, lest she ever offend in speech. Thus, intent upon holy studies and exercises, from being barren she deserved to become a mother, just as almighty God had ordained from the beginning. Therefore the holy woman conceived by a holy husband; she conceived without original stain; she gave birth without fault. O holy and formerly unheard-of conception. She conceived by a man, but this conception was never liable to any crime. She conceived according to the order of nature, but beyond the custom of nature. Holy conception, to be celebrated with continual praises, which prepares a mother [for the Son?], over which the choir of angels rejoices, and the whole world throughout the earth exults. Truly an ever-honored conception, which was pleasing to almighty God before it was fulfilled. Truly worthy conception, which, with the Holy Spirit preserving it, took its beginning in such purity that it was disposed to conceive and bear God. Therefore Anne, the most holy parent, is to be revered by us with the highest devotion, she who conceived the mother of God without stain. What a worthy offering she offered to God when she presented her most holy daughter in the temple. Finally, it pertains to declaring the merits of the holy mother that the daughter whom she conceived and bore she consecrated to the Lord immediately from infancy. As was the mother’s way of life, so was the daughter’s training. No one can teach another what he himself has not learned; no one badly trained trains children well. Often children advance according to the habits of their parents, and what they have seen practiced by them they embrace more willingly. A mother worthy of the most holy daughter: so that from her from whom she had drawn the material of her flesh, from her she might suck the teachings of piety. The grace of God had anticipated both and had filled both; but it was earlier in the mother, more abundant in the daughter. The holy mother taught the daughter what she herself had first learned from her parents, although she had no need of human instruction, whom the Holy Spirit filled at conception. Nor indeed did she need maternal instruction, since she was full of heavenly grace. Learn, all of you, to train your daughters for the honor of God: not to love the pomps of the world, to flee public sight, to remain at home. For the holy bridegroom hates publicity and loves the secrecy of a pure mind. Why do you run about through streets and squares, if you love modesty, virgins? The archangel came to Mary not in public but in secret; not to her speaking in the street, but to her silent in her chamber. The apostles received the Spirit not in the forum, but shut up in the house.

    [unclear] the most blessed virgin learned from her mother, indeed from the Holy Spirit. She carefully kept it. She was accustomed to avoid wandering excursions; Mary remained in a solitary house. Look to both: mothers to the mother, virgins to the virgin. Believe me, it does not befit your honor to delight in public; it is not expedient for virgins to be greeted in the marketplace, because he who frequently goes into public diminishes the reverence of honor. When virginity is modest, it flees the public. Without modesty there is no sincere virginity, nor can one who is too public remain pure.

    That holy mother Anne conceived her daughter, the most blessed Mother of God, without original stain. Chapter 7.

    Since it greatly contributes to declaring the merits of the sanctity of the most blessed mother Anne, that she bore the Mother of God without the stain of original guilt, the prerogative of so great an honor must by no means be passed over by us in silence. And indeed we know that this most pure conception was set as a sign, against which many contradict down to the present day; while they wish to defend the custom of nature, they are not afraid to attack the grace of God. Why do the foolish bark? Why do the unlearned murmur? Is it not permitted to God to do what he wills? Behold, the Church venerates the conception of the Mother of God as pure, without stain; behold, it celebrates the feast with annual devotion, and contentious men labor to stain it with rash presumption. Holy and most learned men, past and present, in various kinds of writing, proclaim in their lucubrations that this conception was never subject to original stain; and still the sons of Adam rashly attack it. Almost all religious orders of diverse kinds confess, believe, and preach that she always existed most pure; to wish to condemn them as erring is extreme madness. Behold, secular men, religious, monks, devout and learned, celebrate in verse and prose the ever most pure conception; and lukewarm and unlearned men, for whom it seems enough to know the name of philosophy, strive to besmirch the holiness of the Mother of God. Many, I say, most learned men have published various treatises in its defense. What learned man has ever written the contrary? But you, indeed unworthy of your name, [Nicator?], who, setting your mouth against heaven, have impiously blasphemed against the most pure Mother of God, will not have done this without God’s grave notice, since you were moved to write not by piety but by impiety. Finally, we know that more than enough answer has been made to your foolish rashness by learned men in various styles of writing. And you depart confounded not by our arms, but by the power of God. Nor do I condemn your error, but your arrogance, your rashness, your presumption. For I know that to hesitate about the conception of the Virgin Mary is not a sin, since God wished it to be hidden; but her

    to attack, and rashly to define what you do not know, is an unheard-of crime. If we are instructed to interpret in the better sense those things whose intention we do not know, how much more ought we to receive with piety the hidden works of God, whose reasons we do not know? None of us was present at the counsel of God; no one has known the manner of the conception. But, induced by many reasons, we, from pious belief, believe that she always existed most pure; the adversaries, led astray by consideration of nature, defend the contrary opinion with rash presumption. But it is better to render an account for piety toward the Mother of God than for rashness.

    If we err, piety, indeed God himself, is the cause; but if you err, O adversaries, say for what cause. What consideration moves you to say so boldly that the most pure conception of the Mother of God was subject to original guilt? You will answer, I know: love of truth. But show that your opinion is true, and I shall believe that you are lovers of truth. Yet you will not show it, because you do not understand. You do not understand because you do not believe. You do not defend the truth, which you do not know; for no one properly defends what he does not know.

    Consideration of human nature deceives you; while you carefully turn over its custom, you do not consider that God is the establisher of nature. He who made nature is above nature. God, the maker of the law, does not confine himself under the condition of human law; but he who willed that a virgin should give birth also preserved her from sin beyond the order of nature. Therefore the cause of the opposing opinion takes its beginning from rashness, and for this reason it does not so much deserve reward as punishment. For just as punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause does, so the error concerning the conception does not condemn [unclear].

    One must believe the examples and testimonies of the ancients. We read that very many have most miserably perished who attacked the purity of the glorious conception; but we find that no defender of it was ever struck by God. For the supreme dignity of the Mother of God, when considered, urges us to the defense of the most holy conception; it shone forth such and so great that it was most worthy of every honor.

    If we are mistaken, we are excused by holy piety. But if you err, who will defend you? Truth? But you do not know it. Justice? But it condemns errors; it does not excuse them. Mercy? But you do not have the bowels of mercy. Who, then, will free you? The Virgin Mary? But you despise her honor. The Son of God? But you do not love his mother. The prayers of the saints? But you detract from their queen. Therefore you will have no excuse, because you offend God and all his saints. You arm yourselves with scholastic arguments, and you are naked of piety. Whatever you bring forward in defense of your opinion is alien to the fear of God; for you do not seek the honor of God, you who attack the purity of his mother. But hear

    my counsel, and change your purpose. Return at last to yourselves, for it is time, and do not presumptuously defend an uncertain opinion, which, without examining it, you can pass over without sin. If you love God, if you love Jesus Christ, the Savior of all, [do not] do so great an injury to his most holy Mother, concerning whom no one is permitted to think [anything but] most holy things. To believe that her conception was always most pure belongs not to necessity but to piety; not to believe it belongs to human slowness. But, by not believing, to attack it, and to wish to defend the contrary opinion, is not only not without fault, but is also a matter of great rashness and folly. For indeed rashness is rightly reproved where piety is rewarded. Let no one think that sin a small thing which is committed against God and his Mother. But he who loves the Son of God does not open his mouth against the honor of his Mother; he does not detract from her purity; he does not stubbornly defend an uncertain opinion. And because where the devotion of the humble receives a reward, the presumption of the proud will find torment. For the Mother of God is believed to have been worthy to be conceived without the original stain, she who, as a virgin, was to bear him who would wipe away the sins of the whole world. Blessed Mother Anna too was worthy of such a conception, whose renowned way of life was most pleasing to God. I do not wish you to wonder that the Mother of God, contrary to the custom of nature, was preserved from original sin, she whom God, the infuser of grace, had prepared as a dwelling for himself. Consider the one born as Mother of God, and you will not wonder at a conception without stain. Great are the things that are said, but true, but holy, but fitting for the Mother of God, whose conception grace anticipated; and at this nature marvels. We too marvel, because we faithfully believe. But the adversaries, not believing, do not marvel, but are confounded. If you can grasp these things, believe; if you do not grasp them, do not examine them, if you do not wish to sin. For it is better to keep reverent silence concerning the purity of the most blessed Mother of God than to speak unworthy things. Take care, therefore, always to honor with humble silence those things which you cannot understand.

    How the most blessed mother Anna presented her sweetest daughter to the Lord in the temple.

    Chapter 8.

    In the beginning of the book of Kings we read that Anna, the wife of Elkanah, offered her son Samuel, whom she had asked from the Lord, to God’s service at the temple after the years of weaning. Indeed, she became so pleasing to God by the offering of Samuel that he not only chose him as priest, after Eli had been rejected, but also filled him with the spirit of prophecy and wisdom. What, brothers, is presented to us by Samuel’s offering by his mother? O how pleasing to almighty God was that offering, in which already then a most worthy dwelling was being prepared for the Only-begotten.

    God had chosen her before the foundation of the world and had pre-elected her, and what he had ordained without time he fulfilled in this presentation. How great, we think, was the joy then in heaven, when Mary, a young virgin, was joined to the heavenly bridegroom. The most holy virgin is led by her mother into the temple, she who was to bear the Lord of the temple; and now, as a little child of three years, she is made ready for divine nuptials. Who will be able to recount your joy then, O mother Anna, when you devoutly handed over to the temple, to serve there, your daughter received from the Lord, indeed the one who was to bear the Lord of the temple? No one ever offered so pleasing a gift to God; no one ever presented to the temple a treasure of so great a price. The holy parents marvel in their daughter at qualities beyond her age; they marvel at her grace; they marvel at her eagerness. For she was full of grace from the womb, nor was she ever subject to any stain, however slight, she who was the temple of God. Why do you marvel at your daughter, mother? The grace of God is not enclosed under the law of nature; the power of the Holy Spirit does not require age to accomplish what it wishes; the gift and will of the Most High is not constrained under many years. The Most High sanctified his tabernacle, and the ark in which he had resolved to place the true manna he most beautifully adorned within and without with the purest gold of virtues. How perfect the mother was in the love of God she declared in this offering of her sweetest daughter. For unless she had been steadfast in the fear of the Lord, she would never have allowed her daughter, beloved as her own life, tender and noble, to be torn from her. But love of the Creator overcame a mother’s heart, and the pledge most dear above all created things she offered with cheerful countenance to the Lord, to be consecrated. Nothing here is done by chance; custom works nothing; all things without time were ordained by the Most High; all things by the counsel of God were foreordained from eternity. O Joachim and Anna, most blessed parents, who were worthy to bring forth her who, without male seed, deserved to beget the Son of God. Truly an offering always to be honored with fitting praises, which provided a mother for God, a queen for the angels, and a savior for the world long lost. Moreover we believe this offering to have been adorned with such purity that under God no earlier one could exist; for she was made queen of the angels, mother of God, lady of the world. In the greatest glory before God, too, these most blessed parents must be believed to be, who begot a mother for the Son of God. Learn, O parents, to set the fear of God before your children; learn to form them when young in the love of God, lest, if you neglect them as little ones, you later find them obstinate. Anna offered her sweetest three-year-old daughter to the Lord; she taught the little child to fear God; she presented her to the temple to be instructed in the fear of the Lord. But you do not do so. You instruct your daughters for dances and the love of worldly vanities; you tell them nothing of the fear of the Lord; you persuade them of nothing concerning eternal life, since indeed you have learned nothing good from your parents. Let not a woman glory in the multitude of her children if she has neglected to instruct them properly in the charity of God, for it is not multitude of children but uprightness that commends women. To God [unclear] your last life. Anna words. [unclear]. [unclear]. [unclear]. [unclear]. Pomona. Concerning Lord. He now. That great woman. That great woman. That great woman. That great woman. I

    That the holy mother Anne is held in the greatest honor with God and all the saints. Chapter IX. We return, however, and hold without any hesitation that holy Anne, the parent of the Mother of God, is of singular merit and honor before God; by this she is not only sufficient for her own glory, but also becomes fit and powerful to bring us aid. For if we trust that the apostles and the other saints are powerful with God, we must necessarily believe that the parents of God are most powerful. For Anne, a most holy woman, pleased almighty God to such a degree that he wished the mother of his Only-begotten to be born from her; he would never have dedicated a womb for his mother unless he had found in it the merit of great holiness. For Scripture says: “The holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, nor will it dwell in a body subject to sins.” In the most blessed mother Anne there was nothing deceitful, nothing that could have offended God, but all things were upright, clean, and holy, and worthy of the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. Therefore she is rightly believed to be next after her daughter in glory before God, since she was able to please him so greatly in this life. Let no foolish disputant object to me that the saints of the Old Testament were of lesser merit than those of the New, since time does not bestow holiness, but the grace of faith. I except Anne, whom I acknowledge as a lover not so much of the Old Testament as of the New. For she herself established the ark of the New Testament, and carried it for nine months in her womb. Nor does time diminish the holiness that God’s special grace has granted. So great a grace had gone before the most blessed Anne that in Israel in her time she had no equal in virtue and holiness. Accordingly it seems fitting that she should prevail before God in glory more than the rest, she who shone before others in life. Indeed, just as the Son of God surpasses his mother [unclear] where virtue abounds, affection does not cease where love is continued; the love of kinship does not perish where glory is owed to merits. Carnal affection ceases where there is no generation of the flesh. But love never ceases where it loves; affection, where love is continued, does not perish; the love of kinship does not perish where glory is owed to merit. I confess that in the blessed carnal affection ceases, and the generation of the flesh also ceases; but the love of kinship does not cease, since among them all it is common. For no one ever hated his own flesh. Nor is the Son of God so harsh that he does not love his holy parents, his own flesh, his own bowels. Or how would he not love his own parents, who loves all his saints and servants? For he says: “I love those who love me.” Who could ever love God according to the flesh more than his parents? From their blood he was incarnate without stain, fed with milk, nourished with care. Far be it, then, that we should think the most blessed Anne of God

    the Son's grandmother [to be] without the greatest honor in the fatherland, she who on earth stood so close to God. If the Lord Jesus, king of heaven, loves those who love him, it is rightly to be believed that he loves his own parents before all others; nor can they be in the heavenly fatherland without special glory, whom almighty God on earth had filled with such extraordinary grace. Therefore we believe Anna, after the Virgin Mother, to be nearest to the Son of God, and a powerful advocate for the wretched, to whom the king of heaven denies nothing, but in all things for which she asks honors her face as that of a most beloved parent. The whole Trinity also loves her; the angelic choir honors her; all the citizens of the heavenly fatherland venerate her with the greatest reverence as the honorable mother of their queen; and not undeservedly. For if they love the king, they rightly venerate his grandmother. The honor that is paid to parents is shown to the children. But he proves that he loves the king less who does not venerate his father and mother and his whole lineage. We are also accustomed to grieve more over injuries done to our parents than over our own. Why is this, unless because an insult inflicted on them groans within us? For we believe that not only our parents but also we ourselves are marked by grave injury in the same way; just as we believe an insult to our parents to be our own, so we reckon the honor shown to them as ours. Whatever honor, therefore, we pay to the divine mother Anna, let us believe without doubt to be shown to God. For the Lord says to us in the Gospel: Whatever you have done to one of the least of mine, you have done to me. If he asserts that everything paid to the least who believe in Christ has been done to himself, how much more must it be believed to be done in those who are not merely least with him, but greatest and most powerful? His parents are not last with the Son of God, not least but greatest, not small but most powerful. Whatever veneration, therefore, we pay to them, let us by no means doubt that it is doubled before God. And if revelations are to be believed, the most blessed Virgin appeared to a certain devout man and, among other things, said to him: If you love me, honor my mother, and whatever reverence you pay to her will be doubly pleasing to me. Now therefore, brothers, if we love the Mother of God, if we desire to please the queen of heaven, let us honor her venerable mother with diligent devotion, and we shall find them both pious helpers in every tribulation. Behold, the angels of God and all the saints venerate and love Anna, and shall we be silent and mute from her honor? The intercessions of the saints are necessary for us, not for those who already exult in the fatherland; and therefore it is fitting that we should always be devoted in their veneration. We, I say, who still live in the flesh and are pilgrims away from the Lord, must honor those citizens of the fatherland above with especial devotion, so that, aided by their suffrages, we may be able to come to the joys which they inhabit. But among all the saints we believe the Mother of God to stand preeminent, and Anna, her venerable parent; if we are devoted to them and their worshippers, no adversities will harm us.

    That the blessed mother Anne is powerful before God to aid those who devoutly call upon her. Chapter X.

    Since the holy and most blessed mother of the Mother of God is, in the kingdom of heaven, very near to the Son of God and to his mother in merits and charity, there is no doubt that she is able to obtain help for our miseries, provided that the devotion of our mind is earnestly directed toward her. She cannot fail to be most merciful, who bore the mother of mercy in her womb. How pious, how powerful, how ready she is to repel human miseries, there are almost as many witnesses as there are devout worshippers found for her. For she is powerful in the palace of the highest emperor, whom God hears as she supplicates, out of reverence for her, and whatever she has asked he grants without delay. Let him doubt her authority and power who does not know that she gave birth to the Queen of Angels. Let him hesitate over the piety of the most blessed mother who is ignorant that the Savior of the world came forth from her most noble blood.

    She is powerful and very near to God; she is pious and inclined toward our necessities; she is accustomed to grant benefits to human beings, so that they may learn continually to hold her many merits in memory and honor. Therefore approach the pious patroness confidently; knock upon her with assiduous prayers, because she is able to obtain pardon for you; she is able to lead you to eternal life. Nothing is lacking to her that can profit our necessities; she has everything that can help us, since the capacity to be able and the piety to be willing are always present in her. Therefore, brothers, let us doubt nothing, let us hesitate at nothing, since sure intercessions will be at hand for us, if firm faith is not lacking. In whatever tribulation we shall cry out to her, we shall find ready help, if we devote faithful service to her name. Do you desire to know, brothers, what this most holy woman is able to provide for you? Listen. Anne drives away sadness, expels the lust of the flesh, relieves poverty, cures infirmities, mitigates adversities, calms oppositions, eliminates vices, plants virtues, enlightens the understanding, purifies affection, remits sins. Therefore, whoever you are who, in good pursuits, have fortune contrary to you; whoever you are who feel the adverse storm of this pilgrimage, call upon Saint Anne with devout and assiduous prayers, knock upon the mother with supplications, and you will find remedies of unexpected consolation. For she herself is a safe refuge for the wretched, a sure remedy for the sick, an unfailing solace for the desolate. Why do you hesitate to approach her, since she is both powerful and willing to help you? Nothing earthly is required of you, not gold, not silver, but only a heart extended in devotion toward God and Saint Anne. Why then are you afraid? Why do you waver:

    Believe me: there is no tribulation, no distress, no necessity that can stand before Anne’s prayers. Whatever weighs upon you, whatever troubles you, whatever is opposed to a good will, refer it to Anne, and [without doubt?] she will deliver you. It is impossible for her not to obtain everything she wishes. The King of heaven is her grandson; he will not be able to deny anything to his most sweet grandmother. The Mother of God is her daughter; she cannot pour out prayers to God in vain. The whole court of the heavenly fatherland loves Anne as a mother, venerates her as a lady. If she asks anything from God, the prayers and vows of all the saints will concur. Blessed is the person who, with continual devotion and assiduous prayers, shall have had Anne as advocate.

    That holy mother Anne, as a most pious advocate, is to be held by us in the greatest honor. Chapter 11.

    With how great honor and how great reverence the most blessed Anne is to be honored by us, we have sufficiently considered from what has already been said, since in the heavenly fatherland she is honored by the supreme God himself and by all the saints with such, and indeed ineffable, proclamations of praise. For if the citizens of that fatherland above, already established in the highest tranquillity, venerate and love her as a most powerful lady, how much more ought we, wretched people still placed amid many tribulations, to invoke and honor her as a pious patroness. Indeed she must be revered by us with the greatest reverence, through whose patronage we can safely escape all the evils of this fleeting world. And truly the mother who bore beneath her breast, enclosed by her womb, the origin of our redemption is ever to be venerated with worthy praises.

    She is rightly, I say, to be honored, because she bore for us the Mother of God without stain, through whom the Son of God, the Savior, came to the world. Therefore, just as we venerate and revere the most blessed parent of God because, an immaculate virgin, she bore the Redeemer for us, so too it is fitting that we honor Anne because she brought forth the mother of our Savior without fault. Unless we had had a mother, whence would the daughter have come? Let no one doubt, let no one waver, let no one seethe with wicked thoughts, because if Anne had not been most holy, she would not have been chosen as mother of the Mother of God. For it was fitting that she who was to give birth to the Mother of God should be adorned with the radiance of every holiness, since she was to become the mother not of just any virgin, but of her than whom, among God’s pure human creatures, none purer or holier could be found.

    Most blessed Anne, therefore, was worthy of this office by God’s gift; she was worthy by the merit of her life; she was also worthy by the testimony of the law. Worthy, I say, was she to bear the Mother of God, because she knew how to love God above all things, because she had learned to keep his law without offense. There was no holier woman in Israel, who may be believed to have been honored by God with such great gifts. Though barren, she conceived from seed, but without stain of seed. She conceived, I say, without the stain of fault, and bore Mary, the devout, most holy, blessed Mother of God.

    Who loves the king and does not honor his parents? Who loves Mary and does not venerate Anne? Let the arguments of vanity be silent; let words of excuse withdraw far away. He is shown to love the Son of God less who does not venerate Saint Anne. Let the person with hardened heart blush, reprobate in regard to piety, who says that he loves the Mother of God and is shown not to love Anne, her mother. It is a foolish and ruinous presumption to take confidence in the daughter’s patronage while scorning to honor her venerable mother. For whoever has the mother hostile will not be able to find the daughter appeased. For the daughter loves the mother, and the whole host of the heavenly court venerates Anne. If anyone has Anne as advocate, he will have all the saints in heaven as patrons. Let us therefore love the mother, dearest brothers, who can bring us into the sight of God. For she is both pleasing and very near to God.

    On the feast and commemoration of most holy Anne, always to be held by us in honor. Chapter 12.

    Finally, if we love Anne, the most fortunate parent of the Mother of God, if we wish to pursue her with fitting honor, it is necessary that we celebrate with yearly devotion her honorable feast, which is on the seventh day before the Kalends of August. Nor should we believe this to be enough for us in accordance with our devotion, unless we hasten to frequent her commemoration more often, as that of a most singular patroness. But if the adversary should falsely wish to object to us the novelty of this feast

    let us reply. We are in no way introducing new feasts, but renewing ancient ones. And I believe I have argued sufficiently about this above; by these arguments I do not doubt that satisfaction has been given to the devout worshippers of Anna. Moreover, to wish to satisfy the curious and the proud is superfluous, since piety does not move them, devotion does not stir them, charity does not inflame them. Therefore let the devout worshippers of blessed Anna believe, and hold without any hesitation, that her feast is ancient and was customarily celebrated by the ancients with the greatest reverence, as befitted the mother of the most holy Mother of God. For in Judea and the regions overseas her commemoration was very famous among faithful Christians, until at length, when the land was occupied by unbelievers, it was for a long time too much neglected. But in the regions of Europe her feast was not so celebrated, because many of these came to the faith later. Yet in certain places of Europe there was always a solemn remembrance of Anna, which had been instituted by the faithful coming from Palestine. This is proved by the altars erected in her honor in various churches from ancient times. This is proved also by very ancient oratories and by various treatises of the fathers on the praises of Anna. But why do we try to defend the antiquity of this feast, which no good and devout person will wish to attack? Against the rebellious we are not at present to dispute, since we shall never be able to persuade them by words to the worship of most holy Anna. Therefore, whether the commemoration of so great a woman is judged by them to be new or ancient matters little; this alone must be labored for by us, that it be celebrated by faithful and devout Christians with all reverence. For if we honor with due devotion the feasts of other saints of Christ, why should we not celebrate the feast of Anna, most beloved by God? For you know that she is inferior to the rest neither in merits nor in glory, since she was of such dignity while still mortal that she bore the mother of him who, immortal, lives forever in heaven. And just as we make some commemoration daily of our special patrons, so also concerning Saint Anna, as right devotion shall suggest, let us offer something of praise to God every day. And if devout worshippers ought always to be ready for her honor, nevertheless on her birthday especially they ought to be solicitous, since her commemoration is observed not only on earth but is also honored in heaven by the votive praises of the saints. It also agrees with devotion and befits piety that, just as the Sabbath day is observed by clergy and people with masses and prayers in honor of the most holy Mother of God, so the commemoration of her mother should be celebrated at least once a week. For by solicitude for household affairs we are quickly distracted from devotion, to which it is necessary that we return at least once a week, lest, if we put off the honor of venerable Anna too long, in our lukewarmness we lose her patronage. For celebrating this weekly remembrance, Tuesday seems sufficiently fitting, on which she is read to have been both born and to have died. Finally, in many places a laudable custom has prevailed that, with no less reverence, the commemoration of Saint Anna is celebrated every Tuesday than the Sabbath day is observed in memory of the Mother of God in the church of the faithful. For we have seen among the Sicambri and [Grunes?] that every Tuesday masses are sung in honor of blessed Anna, lamps are lit, offerings are made, and the poor are more abundantly refreshed. We have also known among them certain devout worshippers of the blessed woman who, in honor of Jesus, Mary, and Anna, every Tuesday lit three candles on her altar, gave three special alms, and received as many acts of pardon or disciplines. This custom took its origin from a miracle of Saint Anna that happened in Pannonia, where she advanced a desolate and very poor young man to great honors and riches. If anyone desires to have knowledge of this matter, let him read the said miracle, which is now so widely known among the worshippers of blessed Anna that it can be hidden from no one. And we have recognized that these things are done by many not only on Tuesday, but every day, as the devotion of each person requires. Therefore priests of the Lord who desire to be devout worshippers of the most holy mother should take care to celebrate devoutly for her commemoration at least once a week. Whoever has adopted that devotion as his custom, we believe that he will have Anna as a pious advocate in every necessity. Therefore let no one be silent from the praise of so great a patroness, let no one grow sluggish in devotion to her, let no one [unclear] her commemoration

    [unclear]. For Anna is interpreted as “grace” or “gift.” It is a name fitting so great a parent, which we believe was given to her at birth not by chance, but preordained by God. For rightly is she interpreted as “grace,” since she was to give birth to the mother of grace. Rightly “grace,” through whose intercession the grace of God is obtained for the faithful. She is also interpreted as “giving” or “gift,” because those whom she finds devoted in her honor she makes rich with many gifts of grace. Rightly “gift,” through whom remission of sins is given. Whoever, therefore, is weighed down by the burden of sins, whoever is struck by the darts of temptations, let him flee trustingly to the aid of mother Anna; let him offer prayers and gifts of devotion, and there will be nothing that can prevail against him for evil.
