For Anna is called “grace”; according to her name she does not cease to obtain the grace requested, if she is found with devout faith. Therefore, faithful people, celebrate most devoutly the feasts of so great a mother; rejoice in her commemoration, and pour out diligent prayers to her, because she is able to free you from every tribulation. Rejoice in the Lord our God, all you who love Saint Anna. Praise the name of the Lord, all faithful peoples, who love the mother of the God-bearer and Virgin. Take Anna as your patroness, honor her with devout prayers, and you will always find her a faithful advocate.

    With what exercises and devotions we ought to honor the most blessed mother Anna. Chapter 13.

    We have heard how greatly the most blessed mother Anna, by her merits, has power with almighty God for those who pray; we know how worthy she is of honor. It remains now that we briefly say how she is to be honored by us. And although, because of the diversity of devotion, no general rule concerning the manner of veneration can be set down by us, nevertheless we shall try, as far as we can, to persuade everyone, so that no one may be able to excuse himself through ignorance from the praise of so great a mother. And indeed, first of all, devotion will establish for each person the manner of praising her; the greater that devotion is, the more useful the manner will be. Just as we are accustomed to venerate the other saints with diverse ceremonies, so also we honor her, but more abundantly. You have the manner: apply your desire. If perhaps I seem too brief to you, receive a fuller manner. If kings, princes, and bishops of churches honor blessed Anna, let them erect chapels and oratories in her memory, institute prebends, and found monasteries. Let them also make diligent prayers to her, celebrate her memory, and feed the poor and needy out of reverence for her. With whatever zeal the faithful venerate the other special saints, let them know that the divine mother Anna is to be honored not with less, but with more abundant zeal. Likewise, let the prelates of the faithful themselves have the same manner of veneration, and let them institute that the feast of the most holy mother Anna be celebrated by all in their dioceses. Let them confer indulgences upon the faithful for the worship of Anna; let them confirm confraternities in her honor, the offerings of prayers in her name

    let abbots also, and the other rulers of monks in their monasteries, devoutly celebrate the memory of Anne; let them build chapels and altars; let them pour forth continual prayers to her. Likewise let the leaders and brothers of the other religious orders do the same as far as they can, and let them never at any time grow lukewarm in the worship of so great a mother. But you, O professors of the Carmelite order, who by the most ancient privilege are specially distinguished by the title of the most blessed mother of God and Virgin Mary: you ought to venerate and embrace most holy Anne with singular devotion, from whose daughter you are called venerable. Take care, therefore, that you never be lukewarm in the worship of the mother, you who from her daughter have obtained the name of so great an honor. You also, all others chosen into the lot of the Lord, extend your souls to the honor of the most holy mother of the mother of God; bestow on her whatever praises you can, and instruct those subject to you, as far as possible, to do the same. You too, O men distinguished by learning in letters, in whom the vein of composition abounds: dedicate your talents to the divine mother Anne; play in verse in her honor, and, as much as you are able, praise her also in prose. But the simpler, whose abilities are slower and not sufficiently suited for composing, should copy out with devotion the things that have been published by others; they should read them more often, and for the edification also of others should affix them to the altars of the holy mother. Let them read prayers suited to her honor; let them read due praises; let them read hymns, songs, and proses. Let no one be free from the praises of Anne; let no one be silent; let no one grow lukewarm. Let all nations redeemed by the blood of Christ celebrate the memory of Anne, from whose merits a great hope of salvation is promised to us. But lest matter for prayer be lacking to the devout worshippers of Anne, three years ago we made, in her honor, a brief prayer in the form of the angelic salutation, which is now both had and read by many. And it seems to us sufficiently fitting that, just as in the rosary of the mother of God we pay five Lord’s Prayers and fifty angelic salutations, so also we should do in honor of Saint Anne, yet in such a way that in place of Ave Maria our prayer which follows should be said.

    Prayer.

    O venerable Anne, mother of the mother of God, most pleasing to the Holy Trinity, honored above all women: blessed are you in the Lord, and blessed is the offspring of your womb, and the virgin-born son of that offspring, Jesus Christ. Amen.

    Many appoint this prayer in honor of Saint Anne in place of the angelic salutation in the rosary, because it is both brief and by no means useless. But if our prayer for the rosary of Saint Anne does not please someone, let him read the salutation, as is the custom, angelic; and at the end, after he has said “Jesus Christ,” let him add this clause: And blessed be your most honorable mother, Saint Anne, from whom your virgin flesh proceeded without stain. Amen.

    The holy mother of God is said to have revealed this clause to a certain recluse devoted to her. If this too does not please someone, let him make, according to his devotion, some other prayer suited to the honors of the most blessed mother Anne, as best he can.

    There are also many other practices of holy exercise, which are placed in each person’s discretion and devotion. A devout mind will always find a way to honor the most holy Anne with due praises. In fasts and tears, in alms and prayers, in genuflections and disciplines, in song and readings, the most blessed mother is to be honored by us. Yet it offends us no little that we find no suitable history of the holy mother, one that would in all respects befit her honor and feast. For the history that is already in use among many, in various forms, is variable and, as it seems to many, not sufficiently elegant; I pass over the fact that it is less worthy of such merits, and in very many places seems apocryphal. Nor is there only one, but several are found, as each person has seen fit, with additions that are less approved. What shall I say of the office of the Mass, which we see confused in many places by similar variety? An office is sung by very many which some devotee drew out from the Saturday office of blessed Mary, changing the meanings of the words but retaining the melody; this seems less conducive to devotion, since hearers, deceived by the similarity of the melody, think that the celebration is not of Saint Anne but of the Mother of God. If the matter is pleasing, let at least the melody be changed. Yet all these things could easily be corrected if the authority of some pontiff intervened; relying on it, men learned in these matters might compose a history and office, regulated in reading and melody and approved by the Scriptures.

    [unclear] rewards her worshippers manifoldly in this life and in the life to come. Chapter 14.

    The frequent display of miracles merits reverence for the saints. Blessed Anne is most worthy of the greatest honor, since she bestows daily so many and such great benefits upon her devout worshippers that there is no one who could recount them all. We indeed know many miracles of Saint Anne, both new and old, but it is not our purpose now to direct the mind to these things, which we have learned are called into doubt by many: not because they contain any falsehood in themselves, but because modern men, most of whom seem learned to themselves, do not believe miracles but disparage them. We therefore do not wish to give an occasion for disparagement, nor to expose the present treatise to suspicion, lest they say that we write not true things but apocrypha. For no one understands, no one believes, no one grasps how great are the benefits that God daily bestows upon the lovers of Saint Anne, unless devout experience instructs him. We know, however, that through the invocation of Saint Anne many powerful, learned, noble, and ignoble men, virgins and women, young people and old, have often been delivered from very great tribulations, rescued from dangers, and wonderfully aided in necessities; also many religious persons of either sex

    and secular persons too, we have very often found to have been delivered, by Anne’s merits, from the gravest temptations of flesh and spirit; others, placed in need and poverty, to have been unexpectedly and abundantly provided for through Anne’s intercessions; others to have been cured of grave calamity. Who could enumerate how many have been healed, by the aid of the most dutiful mother Anne, from destructive sadness of mind and melancholy? How many also have escaped secure amid adversities, fearless amid enemies and robbers, safe amid the dangers of the sea? The most holy mother Anne has been accustomed to rescue many devoted to her from various [unclear], to free them from the contagion of pestilence, and also to cure them of various infirmities. Who could tell how many she has brought back from the worst despair to the hope of mercy; how many she has recalled from the hardest habit of sin to the paths of penitence; how many, living lukewarmly in religion and outside it, she has inflamed with the fire of divine love? By her merits and intercessions women in childbirth, otherwise near to death, have been delivered, and many have even been snatched, as we read, from the sentence of eternal damnation. Finally, it is said that she has guarded some of her worshippers from the reproach of infamy; she is remembered to have delivered others from a desperate illness, some from chains and prisons, and certain others from the dangers of imminent death. We also read that by her merits some have been recalled from death to life; others, at the point of death, have been most mercifully visited through her, and before they left the world were already made secure concerning heaven. Often, too, she is said to have illuminated the dulled wits of some, so that those who before had been despised for lack of learning afterward became an object of admiration to many. Orators also, often faltering in speaking, she is said, when invoked, to have strengthened so greatly that they found themselves made not only steadfast but also readier in delivering a speech. Thus, finally, the [unclear] through Anne is immense. For if I had a voice of iron and a hundred tongues, I could not run through all Anne’s benefits by which she is accustomed to aid her worshippers. Indeed, as many are her benefits as there are hardships of human life. In whatever tribulation anyone cries to her with devotion, he can obtain help. She extinguishes the flames of carnal desire; she turns destructive sadness of mind into saving joy; she grants what is necessary for life; she preserves a good and fair reputation. She delivers women in danger in childbirth, mitigates pains, drives away demons. In tribulation it is permitted for a person to seek [her]. Only let devout faith commend the one who prays. But concerning all the things which, in recalling them by category, we have merely touched on, we have at hand particular examples of deeds done, by which we could write not uncertain things, but relate deeds in truth. Yet it is not our purpose to weave a history, but, as much as we can, the praises of the divine mother Anne—

    [unclear] to declare with simplicity. For I would not have said that she is to be venerated on account of miracles, but because of piety toward God. So many and so great miracles concerning our blessed Anne have become known to me that, if I wished to write them all, it would compel me to enlarge this treatise too much. The greatest of divine miracles is this: if by her merits we may deserve to receive compunction and pardon for our sins; if to overcome an evil habit; if to attain eternal life. For this end, and no other, she is to be venerated by us.

    Chapter XV

    On the brotherhood of the most blessed mother, how useful and necessary it is, especially in our times.

    For in these last days, as charity grows cold among many, iniquity abounds. It is very necessary for us, my brothers, that just as we fall almost daily by sinning, so also through frequent devoted exercises of holy practice we may be renewed every day in every good will. For there has never been any institution so holy among human customs that it has not, with time, grown lukewarm from its first fervor. Thus all the orders of religious, declining with the passage of time, have departed from their first institution; unless by the diligence of their superiors they had often been reformed to the paths of regular life, they would always have remained in their deformity. The same thing is also done among Christians, who today are found to have fallen far away from the first institution of the faith.

    Where now is the former [unclear] of our faith? Charity has grown cold, and all the pursuits of religion have likewise perished along with it from among people, for the most part. Who would believe how great a loss evil morals have brought upon the Christian faith? Behold, with God permitting it because of the crimes of men, the unbelieving Saracens, Turks, Tartars, and the other enemies of the Catholic faith, after slaughtering Christians, have brought Asia, Africa, Greece, the Hellespont, and a great part of Europe under their power, so that a twentieth part of the world which once was Christian is not Christian today. And truly, unless the compassion of almighty God preserves the remnants left in Europe, there will soon be an end of the Christian name.

    Since, therefore, weighed down by our sins, we are not sufficient to obtain God’s mercy, the intercessions of the saints must be implored for us with diligent prayers, so that, appeased by their merits, the eternal judge may grant us pardon and peace, which we do not deserve. And lest devotion fail in time, as is customary, we must work with great care so that through the mutual exhortation of the brothers it may attain perseverance.

    Hence a praiseworthy custom has grown up in the Church of God: that the faithful establish congregations in honor of certain saints, which, for the increase of devotion, they call brotherhoods. Thus knights act in honor of Saint George; archers, of Sebastian the martyr; pilgrims, of James the Apostle from Galicia.

    Now therefore, if we believe that these and similar confraternities of the saints are useful for obtaining God’s mercy for the people, we trust that those which are instituted in memory of the most blessed Mother of God and of Anne, her most holy mother, are incomparably better. For as much as the Mother of God, together with her venerable mother, surpasses the other saints in heaven in merits and holiness, so much the more eminent a place does a confraternity dedicated to her name hold. Hence the faithful, moved by pious devotion, in order that they might deserve to have her as a ready advocate before God, instituted in her honor a confraternity under the name of the Rosary; and this has now become so widespread through the various regions of the world that there is scarcely any province in which they do not have several.

    But devout worshippers of the most blessed Anne, considering that from these confraternities the devotion of the faithful could profit, thought to establish, after the example of the Rosary, a praiseworthy congregation in honor of the holy mother, so that the name and praises of so great a patroness might be able to come to the knowledge of many. Accordingly this holy confraternity began in the diocese of Osnabrück, and, confirmed by Conrad, bishop of the said church, almost ten years before this under Frederick III, and, as is reported, approved by miracles, it greatly multiplied. Then Rumold of Laupach, prior of the Carmelite convent of Frankfurt, a very great worshipper and lover of the divine mother Anne, at the urging of certain [unclear], instituted the same confraternity in his aforesaid convent; Berthold of Henneberg, most reverend archbishop of the church of Mainz, confirmed it, and the supreme pontiff Innocent, in the eighth year of his pontificate, approved it by apostolic authority.

    And indeed it is a worthy institution, that the Carmelite brothers, who are especially distinguished by the title of the most blessed Mother of God, should also be more ready in the praises of her mother. Today there is a great and abundant number of persons of both sexes in this confraternity, who daily do and expend many remarkable things for the honor of Saint Anne. But in various places this same venerable confraternity is established by the faithful and celebrated with fitting devotion. Yet there are found good detractors, who tear it with impious teeth and attack it with wicked presumption. What displeases you in this most holy confraternity, O profane detractors? What do you have against it? Bring it forward, so that I may hear.

    You say: “These confraternities are superstitious, because they make the Catholic faith weak, withdraw the worship owed to God, and despise obedience to parish churches. Moreover,” they say, “they deny the customary and due offerings to their priests, offer abundant gifts to monks and their confraternities, and leave their mother churches empty and ruinous.” These are the heads of the opposing party, the charges of an unjust accusation, the objections of wicked detraction. To these we shall reply briefly in order.

    This fraternity of the most blessed mother Anne is not superstitious, as you say, O impious slanderers, but it is true, upright, holy; in it the worship of God is not diminished but increased, obedience is not despised but commended. Nor is the Catholic faith weakened through this holy fraternity, as you think, but renewed and defended, while through the exercises of holy charity it is illumined as being formed.

    But as for your lament that parish churches are deserted, this is to be imputed in no small measure to your own offenses: you exact milk and wool from the sheep of the Lord, yet you do not feed the sheep themselves as you especially ought, nor do you guard them. Why do you pretend that offerings are denied to you, when you abound in many riches? Christ is the vicar of all pastors; if he has wished the faithful to be free in hearing masses, there is no one who can prevent him. You have not seen all the privileges of the monks, nor will you see them. Who does not know that you wage war against holy fraternities for the sake of your purses, and that you tear at monks not from love of God but of gold?

    Behold, the supreme pontiff has confirmed this fraternity; behold, Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, than whom there is no other more excellent, has approved it by ordinary authority; and you foolish men still murmur. Cease, I beg you, cease from this folly, and do not censure what you know such great pontiffs to have approved. Believe me, it is not good to wish to forbid so greatly the devotion of men toward holy Anne. He approaches the greatest confusion who opens his mouth against holy Anne. If you do not believe my words, observe those who are such, and by experience you will know that I have spoken truly.

    It is rash to censure a good that is seen to redound to salvation for many. Many good things come to devout men from the celebration of this most blessed fraternity, of which those who are strangers to it are for the most part empty. It also draws its worshipers to love of God and neighbor; it creates concord of brotherly love; it calls back from vices and sins; it inflames desire for the love of heavenly happiness. I pass over how many masses, how many prayers, how many alms, how many [unclear] it kindles in the minds of all, with how great devotion, how great peace and how great concord might redound in the Catholic Church. For indeed, if all were to come together into this fraternity, it could happen that, for love of holy Anne, they would desist from mutual injuries and be made more ready in observance of the commandments of God. For true fraternity cultivates and nourishes brotherly love, nor does devotion allow those to be unlike whom the observance of so great a congregation has made concordant in the love of most holy Anne. O who would grant that this holy fraternity be spread and celebrated throughout the whole Christian world, so that all the faithful in

    may be seized by love of blessed Anne, and while in holy unity they [unclear], may they rest from wars and mutual insults out of reverence for so great a patroness. Clearly useful and always to be honored is the brotherhood, which gives form to faith by works, raises up hope, stirs charity, inflames devotion. For through it sluggishness is shaken from the minds of the faithful, and the fervor of holy renewal is inspired. Whoever attacks it is mad; whoever speaks against it is more demented than the demented; whoever strives to destroy it envies Christian salvation. And much still remained to be said, had not the occupation of my household affairs claimed me for itself. Whatever I have said against its adversaries has been brought forward not in a spirit of invective, but with the intention of correcting and amending. Yet I trust that there are few who set themselves against the holy mother and her brotherhood.

    Conclusion of this work and excuse for the author's insufficiency, with exhortation of the brotherhood. Chapter XVI.

    Although at the beginning I had proposed to describe more things concerning the praises of the most holy mother Anne, nevertheless from this point it has now pleased me to cease, lest, if I extended the treatise to an immense length, I should choke the reader's devotion by excessive prolixity. For those who wish to persuade others ought to be found brief in speech and abundant in the majesty of their thoughts. From the first I am by no means confident that I have strayed; but how I have fared in the second will be judged by those who are going to read this poor lucubration of ours, such as it is. I have satisfied my promise; I have also satisfied my friends; but neither my devotion nor the dignity of the subject has been satisfied. I wished more than I could, and I did less than I wished. Finally, who can adequately venerate with worthy praises Anne, parent of the most blessed mother of God? Therefore I confess myself unworthy to speak of the most holy mother, since I am a sinful man and entangled in offenses from my youth. Yet I could not be silent from her praise, because necessity lay upon me, and devotion, strongly hemmed in by the prayers of friends, pressed me. But after I had come thus far, the excellence of the subject matter oppressed me, impatient of the heat of summer, so that henceforth I ought to honor with silence her whom I am not able to praise. Whatever, however, has been said and written by me in this work, I submit to the holy Roman Church and to all Catholic learned men, from whose definitive judgment I never intend to dissent. Whatever the sacrosanct Roman Church determines must be believed will be for me the firmest faith. Lastly, we turn our discourse to you, friends, devotees, brothers and sisters of the most holy mother Anne, asking that, receiving in good part those things which have been written by us out of great devotion to the praise of so great a mother, you assail the holy patroness with devout prayers, so that with her accustomed kindness she may come to our aid, wash away our faults, obtain virtues, and win eternal life. We also exhort you to take care to persevere in the love and brotherhood of the most holy mother, honoring her with continual praises, so that, absolved from your faults by her merits, you may lead a tranquil life here and, after this life, an eternal one.

    Here ends the book of lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, on the praises of Saint Anne.

    There follows a tetrastich on the most holy mother Anne.

    [unclear]

    Tetrastich of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the most holy mother Anne.

    Anne, venerable mother of the kindly Virgin, excellent in merits and powerful in piety, no one departs sorrowful who honors and venerates you; for you bring to all the gentle aid of salvation.

    Distich of the same, which he placed at the image of Saint Anne.

    Whoever in adversities has assailed holy Anne with devout prayers, he will be well protected.

    Tetrastich of Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet laureate, on Saint Anne.

    Anne has never dismissed anyone's prayers empty, but, radiant, has always brought the desired aid. Therefore let us heap great honor upon the loving mother, who permits no one's prayers to be empty.

    Tetrastich of Theodoric Gresemund the Younger of Mainz to Saint Anne.

    Anne, parent of the Virgin Mary, hail, auspicious one, worthy to begin the work of our salvation. Since human redemption was begun through you, I pray, continue, covering our crimes with your prayers.

    Distich of Rodolphus Langius, canon of Munster, on Saint Anne.

    Great parent Anne of the second Virgin, hear the pregnant women who bring vows to you with the womb.

    Tetrastich of Jodocus Badius of Ghent on Saint Anne.

    Anne, glory of the world, mother of the mother of Jesus, may your grandson, for the merits of his mother, grant you the stars. Holy Anne, bringing forth the first fruits of our salvation, help us with your offspring and with your grandson.

    Rodolphus Agricola, in his poem on Saint Anne, among other things, says thus.

    Di

    Anne, parent, venerable mother of the highest parent, you who first open for peoples the path of salvation: from you all diseases flee, and pallor and pain, and all harmful things that settle in soul and body. Whatever there is among human beings that wearies cares and hearts flees you, as clouds driven by the winds are wont to do. Rutgerus [Venrai?], regular canon of [Hayn?], to the image of Saint Anne.

    Here pour out deep prayers, devoutly, with knee bent, where Anne the parent sits with her blessed offspring. Do not doubt: you will obtain whatever you ask of her, for Anne continually shines, powerful in prayers.

    Distich of the same author on Saint Anne

    Hail, Anne, mother of the mother of Jesus Christ, and, we ask, drive every wickedness from us.

    The rosary of Jodocus Beissel, patrician of Aachen, on Saint Anne, to the Reverend Father Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict.

    Whoever wishes to read this rosary out of devotion in honor of the most blessed mother Anne should place before it the Lord's Prayer with the salutation of Saint Anne, which he should always repeat after two verses. That salutation is as follows.

    O venerable Anne, mother of the Mother of God, most pleasing to the Holy Trinity, honored above all women: blessed are you by the Lord, and blessed is the offspring of your womb, and Jesus Christ, born of the offspring of the Virgin. Amen.

    Our Father. Hail, [mother] of God.

    Anne, may I, wretched as I am, be allowed to utter your praises, for to you, if you permit it, I shall bring garlands and roses. Anne, you shine, venerable offspring of the kings of Judah, and also renowned through your pious husband Joachim, the sole glory of married women, and their one honor. Pious Anne, you seek offspring not for vain uses, but so that with holy posterity she may worship God. "Rejoice," he says; "behold, exulting mother, you shall have offspring." Anne, you will bear offspring blessed with such great virtue that, though a mother, she will gleam with virginal honor. Hail. Hail. [unclear]. Hail.

    Anne, you will [bear?] the gracious one whom the world does not contain; God himself willingly enters the chaste womb. Hail. Anne, at last from your blood will arise that blood which, when poured out, will bring hope forever to wretched sinners. Hail. Anne, so great an expectation befitted your childbearing; it is by no means easy to be held the mother of the mother of God. Anne, the praises of your offspring will fly above the stars, and all ages will proclaim you happy also.

    Our Father. Hail, [mother] of God.

    Anne, you are believed to have conceived Mary pure from evil, and soon to have had her holy for God. Hail. Anne, in your womb you carry her whom figures marked as coming, whom the holy fathers sang of. Hail. Anne, you carry the enclosed paradise, the happy tree of life, and one sacred with all the honor of the field. Hail. A burning cherub guards it night and day. Anne, you carry a flower that surpasses white lilies, and lowly violets, and the crimson rose. And the golden urn of heavenly bread lies there. Hail. Anne, you carry the bride of the true Solomon, adorned with every jewel, within and without the house. Anne, you carry the temple whose inner chambers sweet sounds and all rejoicing music have filled. Hail. Anne, you carry the veil under a beautiful image, holding in itself the deeds of the fathers, which covers the deep things of God. Hail. Anne, you carry the offspring whose head Phoebus' golden flame clothes, and whose snowy feet the shining moon clothes. Hail.

    Our Father. Hail, [mother] of God.

    Anne, now made possessor of longed-for Mary, you scarcely contain in your whole breast the joys that have sprung up. Hail. Anne, all the stars applauded Mary newly born, and an unwonted radiance flowed from the pole. Anne, it is right to believe that angelic choirs around you celebrated the birthday of your child. Hail. Anne, why do you fear to handle the heavenly girl? She smiles on her mother; she does nothing sorrowful. Hail,

    Anne, take courage; behold, your daughter stretches toward your milky breasts. Hail. Your daughter seeks your tender hands and your neck. Hail. Anne, you break off delays; baring breast and bosom, Hail, you receive her tender little limbs in your tender lap. Hail. Anne, you cherish your daughter, and from your breast the sweet juices, Hail, she draws with rosy mouth, sounding pleasing murmurs. Hail. Anne, if you knew what great sorrows your daughter will bear, Hail, and how many deaths she will bear, you would now be no more. Hail. Our Father. Hail of God.

    Anne, it is dear to your heart to adorn your daughter with approved, Hail, virtues, and to fit her for the highest God. Hail. Anne, you prepare to carry your daughter into the lofty shrine, Hail, but the kindly girl of her own will reached the upper step. Hail. Anne, with slow step and effort you follow the swift girl, Hail, and the eager little virgin consoles her weary mother. Hail. Anne, why do you marvel at strength in the tender virgin? Hail, you see not human things, but holy signs of God. Hail. Anne, you are accustomed to give gifts to the needy and to sacred temples. Hail. Now you give that than which no woman has given more. Hail. Anne, where you wished your consecrated daughter to dwell, Hail, she gladly entered the cloisters and the virginal house. Hail. Anne, about to send away the holy one, your cheeks and eyes with weeping, Hail, you consume; deep love holds you unmoved. Hail. Anne, return home; send your daughter to the Thunderer. Hail. [unclear]. Hail. Anne, let your daughter fly through the ethereal retreats. Hail. Let love, sent from the highest summit, possess her for love. Hail. Anne, it is enough for you that two Marys serve you. Hail. They too will honor you with no small piety. Hail. Our Father. Hail of God.

    Anne, by your own weeping you have learned to aid one who weeps. Hail. Hence you too readily favor the wretched man with prayers. Hail. Anne, you are accustomed to overturn the fixed laws of nature, Hail, and so you will: let the barren woman now be a joyful mother. Hail. [unclear]. Hail. Anne, you drive away disgrace; you give the gifts of fair fame. Hail. You relieve grief, and love yields to you. Hail. The savage chains of a dark prison hold fast. Hail. Anne, be present as a star of relief to suffering mortals. Hail. With you as guide, lost life returns to the languishing. Hail.

    Anne, mother, the sailor calls on you amid the fearful wave, Hail, if winds and water toss his shattered ship. Hail. Anne, mother, you are ever to be feared by the black tyrant. Hail. As ice flees fire, that harmful one flees you. Hail. Anne, mortal hearts cannot ask anything of you in vain; Hail, whatever you will, your daughter and God will will. Hail. Anne, therefore, blessed in merits and in so great an offspring, Hail, great mother Anne, look upon our prayers. Hail.

    Prayer to be said after the rosary

    Almighty and most loving God, who deigned to choose blessed Anne as mother of the mother of your Son, graciously grant that we who honor her memory with faithful devotion may, by her merits and prayers, obtain the helps of eternal life. Through [the same].

    Here ends the rosary of Jodocus Beisselius, professor of both laws and patrician of Aachen, addressed to the reverend father and lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim of the Order of Saint Benedict. From Aachen, on the third day before the Ides of April, in the year 1493.

    Poem of Adam Wernher of Themar on the most holy Anne, addressed to the reverend father and lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot

    In praise of the illustrious grandmother we compose; dear Jesus, grandson, move the plectra of the heart, nor you, daughter, chaste mother, be absent from the singing choir.

    Anne, offspring of kings, long remains barren to her husband; weeping, she laments herself as fruitless; weeping, she prays for offspring.

    Heavenly messengers promise a child; pregnant, joined to her husband, then as a woman in childbed, she is proved a mother by the offspring through whom our salvation comes.

    Thus the venerable stock of Jesse grew green; he becomes worthy, removing the reproaches of the priest. Thus, Anne, prepare us to carry pure prayers to your grandson.

    Commend [us] to the boy whom holy chastity bore of his mother; we ask in prayer, O blessed matron. Christ denies you nothing. To Christ, who, sharing rule with the Father and the Spirit, reigns, be glory through all ages; whom your prayers, O Anna, make reconciled to us. Amen.

    This hymn is sung to the tune of that one which, on the Nativity of Saint Mary, is used in many churches, and begins, “Rejoice, mother, in your inmost heart,” etc. From the castle of Heidelberg, 3 days before the Kalends of February, 1493.

    The Poem or Hymn of John of [unclear] on Saint Anna, to the reverend lord father John Trithemius, abbot.

    Rejoice, Anna, refuge for the wretched. We run to you, we sing, we bring forth songs. On the feast, be gracious with your offspring; now we speak praises to you.

    Rejoice, earth shining, fertile with grass, and wet with rain, with divine dew, from which was born, purer than the ether, the Virgin innocent of sin.

    Rejoice, you who had been of royal seed, now conceived, given to a husband, you had led a chaste marriage, long without offspring, made a mother by vow.

    Rejoice, you who, reddened by the priest’s reproach, are confounded; you call upon God with tears. Heard, you receive your husband coming to meet you at the gate called Golden.

    Rejoice, you who, joyful, embraced Joachim, your husband coming to meet you, and taught by the heavenly deity; and thus the mother of your Jesus is conceived in your little womb.

    Rejoice, wise angelic simplicity, you who, praised by the choir and [unclear] threefold, divide your goods among the temple and the poor, and a part among your servants.

    Rejoice; the people of the faithful celebrate your feasts, so that, as their patroness, you may render the Spirit with the Father, and Christ the Son, by your prayers, propitious, Anna. Amen.

    This hymn takes the melody of the one sung for the Ascension of the Lord, namely “Now the celebrated feast,” etc., and of that one for martyrs, “The illustrious merits of the saints,” etc. From Heidelberg, the third day before the Nones of February, in the year 1493.

    An elegiac poem on Saint Anna by Rutger of Venray, canon regular in Heinau, of the diocese of Worms.

    Hail, splendid mother of the Virgin Mother, of the Father’s splendor, of the brightness of untouched light. You, holy one, bore for the Lord the divine maiden, from whom came forth Jesus, the kindly light of the world.

    Constantly tell your daughter’s son to [unclear] the groaning, although he himself made the heavens and the earth. Your grandson in the flesh, Jesus himself, joined highest divinity to flesh, for he is God and man.

    Therefore, although Jesus always existed, nevertheless he desires and deigns to be called your grandson. Do not hesitate to strike such a grandson with prayers; Anna, we ask, you who will obtain all things asked.

    If he has not bent easy ears to the first requests, Anna, quickly turn again to your daughter. Let your daughter show her breasts to Christ her son; at once the kindly parent will grant what is desired.

    If the matter is very difficult to obtain by prayer, let the daughter with her mother seek help. My faith is firm, nor do I doubt that immediately the Lord will hear both as they pray with gracious ear.

    Therefore, brothers, with continual prayers one must seek the help of Anna and Mary together. It is certain: if you honor the mother of the Lord’s mother, you yourself cherish the titles of the Virgin Mother.

    Again, if you venerate the mother of the Lord, it is clear [unclear]. Let praise, virtue, and honor be to the daughter, to the son, and to Anna, and to the highest Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

    A Sapphic poem of John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the day of Saint Anna.

    Let us celebrate the feasts of holy Anna, of the exalted mother, renowned for merits, who brought forth for the world the parent of God the Father’s Son.

    Her life, ever to be venerated by us, is deservedly praised as blessed; by the gift of signs she increases relief for wretched minds.

    She heals the languid, purges all evils, brightens the hearts of the sorrowful with joy, sets right what is apt, rules and governs, levels rough things.

    Sitting in the palace of the all-powerful highest King, she wipes away stains, sins; she confers grace, and leads faithful souls to the stars.

    We brothers, here frequenting your feasts, bringing vows, praying good things from you: help your servants, refresh, govern us, renowned mother.

    May honor and virtue be to the thundering one above, who, God simple and likewise threefold, granted the crown of great glory to Anna forever. Amen.

    This Sapphic hymn is sung to the melody “with loosened...” etc.; “Life, offspring of the holy Virgin”; “Because the choirs of bards”; “This confessor,” and similar hymns which are Sapphic only. From Sponheim, in the Nones of July, in the year of the Lord 1493.

    An elegiac poem on Saint Mother Anna by John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim.

    How great the rewards are that Anna gives back to her worshippers, no one grasps in mind nor can speak with the mouth. She drives away hardships, obtains pardon, increases the ornaments of honor for her own, and makes them be in heaven.

    By contrast, many very bitter things accompany the scorners of Mother Anna; look out for yourself, wicked one. She crushes the proud, casts down the powerful from honor, and permits them often to suffer great scandals.

    This is clear and remains firm: Anna offers joyful things to those who worship her, but brings back many sad things to her enemies.

    Therefore, men, I advise you: serve so great a patroness, and let the women’s choir likewise be present together in love. What we write is clearly established by examples. Let open ears receive what delights pious hearts.

    From Spanheim, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, 1494.

    A Sapphic Poem by Rutger Sicambrius, for a Hymn in Praise of Saint Anne

    We sing your praises, venerable Anne; favor the measures of those who praise you, obtaining pardon for all, granting the rewards of salvation.

    You, Anne, parent of Christ’s mother, shining in the highest citadel of heaven, obtain whatever you ask of the offspring of the omnipotent one.

    You heal the sick; you wipe away stains; you make faithful servants attain their vow; at last you grant them to climb to the heavenly kingdom.

    By your approved morals you moved the highest Lord, Anne, and by many prayers, that he should grant you to become the parent of so great an offspring in the world.

    To the highest Father, to the heavenly Son, to the Holy Spirit be honor and power, brightness, virtue, devotion, and strength through all ages.

    Another by the Same

    Let us all resound the diligent praises of Anne, mother of the Virgin Mother, with all our powers, from the marrow of the soul, with sonorous voice.

    She brought forth for the wretched race, stained by the blemish of Eve our mother, a noble offspring, the radiant beam that she gave to the world.

    This light of the world drove out the darkness of the blackening world, shining on all with heavenly light, as holy John resounds in the sacred book.

    Anne, mother of the divine maiden, whose grandson you call the groaning one, only according to the flesh: do not spurn the people who pray.

    Virgin, favor us by the intent prayers of Anne, your mother, who entreats for us; you, grandson Jesus, graciously fulfill her prayer.

    To the Son born of Anne’s daughter, together with God, be the highest honor and power; to the blessed Spirit let equal honor be given for all time.

    Another Iambic Dimeter Poem by the Same, Which Is Sung to the Melody of the Hymns of Ambrose

    Bent low, let us honor the feast of blessed Anne, singing due thanks with our voices and with our inmost hearts.

    She is the mother of the nurturing Virgin, who brought forth the light of the world; she is the one who by her virtues made herself most pleasing to God.

    She drives away delays; she confers grace by her prayers; she relieves the most dreadful diseases, both of body and of spirit.

    In praise of her, O King of heaven, to you with sonorous songs, and to the Son and likewise to the Spirit, we pour forth pious praises. Amen.

    An Alcinian Poem by the Same, Which Is Sung to the Melody “Crux fidelis” or “Pange lingua”

    With harmonious voice, with vows and with pious hearts, this feast of Anne the mother, so illustrious, grows eager to set forth. We beg that you be gently present to those who praise you.

    You are the parent of Mary’s mother; you are most pleasing to God. You preserved the ordinances of the law which Moses once delivered to the fathers of old and to the Hebrew peoples.

    Wondrous, gracious gifts you obtain for the faithful, by prayer pleasing before the Son of the high Father. You heal the sick, and grant that hearts be chaste.

    We ask you, Father, and the Son with the Spirit, that you grant joyful things to us who sing together the praises of the renowned, most sweet Anne, the mother of the nurturing Virgin. Amen.

    A Poem by Rutger Venray, a German Regular Canon of Heinsberg, on the Book Concerning the Praises of Saint Anne

    Whoever you may be, reader of this excellent book, put aside empty fear; no frivolous things hold it. This book, pregnant with wondrous meaning and sweet with charm, Abbot Trithemius brought forth by his art, watching over books, guardian of the sheep of Spanheim, who cultivates the sacred writings of the threefold tongue.

    Here you will find the titles of Anne, full of reason and art; only turn them over in a pious heart. He does not follow vain and doubtful little tales everywhere; he teaches the clear streams of sacred eloquence. Therefore, I pray, read lovingly the worthy praises of venerable Anne, which the learned man has brought forth for you.

    Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to the Reader: Greeting.

    When recently, at the insistence of friends, I had resolved to write something concerning the praises of the most holy mother Anne, certain fathers of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary, ever Virgin, of Mount Carmel, asked that I not omit a defense of the most pure Marian conception. And so, persuaded by their prayers and otherwise by just reason, the seventh chapter of this work, concerning the conception

    I have noted beforehand concerning the mother of God and virgin, so that no one may take it otherwise than my intention has it; I thought the reader should be warned. For I know, and it does not escape me, how many most holy and most learned men once wrote that the Mother of God was subject to the stain of original sin, men who flourished long before the Council of Basel. Their opinion, making allowance for the time, I pass over wholly untouched, and I in no way intend to say or write anything against them. Indeed, if anything spoken by me seems rather harsh, let it be referred not to those who think otherwise than we do, but only to the obstinate, who, prattling without learning, do not hesitate to call the defenders of the other opinion heretics. And my words indicate this, since they denote the present time and not the past. For when I say what the foolish bark, what the unlearned mutter, that belongs to the present time, not the past, and today it reproves the obstinate, not those of old who held a different opinion. But when I ask what learned man has ever written the contrary, I am not speaking of the ancient fathers, but I mean those who, after the determination of the aforesaid council, hold a different opinion. Thus I censure only the obstinacy of certain unlearned men of this time, not the opinion of any learned men whatsoever who think differently, since I am not ignorant of the declaration of Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff. But it has seemed to me in no way alien to the holy Roman Church to hold the faith of the most pure conception, which she believes and venerates, as is shown today by many proofs. Finally, together with the doctors of the universities of Paris, Cologne, Heidelberg, Erfurt, Vienna, Tübingen, Ingolstadt, Basel, Mainz, and many others, and with almost all orders and the faithful of Christ spread throughout the whole Christian world, I do not fear to venerate as pure the conception of the Mother of God and Virgin Mary. Yet I do not admit obstinacy, but I wish in all things to obey the Roman Church as the most reverend mother of all churches. This is the pure and sincere intention of my aforesaid chapter, in which I think no one who holds an opinion soberly and without obstinacy is disparaged. Farewell, reader.

    This letter of the aforesaid lord Johannes, abbot, is lacking in certain copies through carelessness and negligence; nevertheless he ordered it to be appended to all copies, and decreed that it be regarded as appended to each.

    Printed at Leipzig by Melchior Lotter.
